planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Voodoo carries some of the darkest flower color found in the genus and benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the petals from bleaching.

directions: Voodoo is grown for its unusually deep, blood-red to burgundy bell-shaped flowers, a striking departure from the pinks, oranges, and yellows more typical of flowering maple, set against plain mid-green maple-like foliage on an upright, well-branched shrub. It flowers heaviest from late summer into fall and continues sporadically through mild winters in the Gulf South. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and pinch young stems to build a fuller, more floriferous framework rather than a single leggy cane. Where hard freezes occur, treat as a cut-back perennial or overwinter a container specimen under cover, since top growth is killed well before the roots.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; a long-cultivated English selection dating to the mid-20th century, grown for its warm brick-red pendent flowers.

directions: Ashford Red is an old, dependable flowering maple selection prized for its deep, old-brick-red bell flowers, produced in flushes from spring through autumn against plain pale-green foliage on an erect, somewhat spreading evergreen shrub. Left unpruned in mild, frost-free climates it can become quite large over years, so an annual spring cutback keeps it compact, dense, and better-flowered rather than open and woody. Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it some afternoon shade relief in the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer. It is killed to the ground by hard freezes but reliably resprouts from mulched roots in zone 8, while colder gardens should grow it as a container plant brought under cover for winter.

common_name: Cannington Carol Abutilon (Gold-Mottled Variegated Flowering Maple)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; part of the Cannington series bred in Somerset, England for its dramatically mottled, virus-variegated foliage.

directions: Cannington Carol is grown chiefly for its foliage — dark green leaves heavily marbled and speckled with gold and cream, a naturally occurring variegation pattern caused by a mild, cosmetically-harmless virus — with scarlet, bowl-shaped flowers appearing as a secondary bonus through the warm months. Its compact, densely branched habit stays smaller and tidier than many flowering maple cultivars, making it a good choice for containers or the front of a tender border where the bright foliage carries the display even between flushes of bloom. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the brightest variegation with a few hours of direct morning sun. Pinch regularly to keep growth dense, and protect from hard freezes since it holds no more cold tolerance than other tender abutilons.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Moonchimes stays more compact and bushy than many flowering maple cultivars, suiting containers as well as mixed borders.

directions: Moonchimes bears soft, pale primrose-yellow, cup-shaped flowers that hang in drooping profusion against plain green, maple-shaped leaves on a naturally bushy, well-branched plant. Its restrained, compact size compared to larger abutilon cultivars makes it easier to keep tidy in a container or foundation planting without heavy pruning. Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest part of the season to prolong flower color. It flowers from spring into fall and draws hummingbirds steadily; expect frost to kill top growth in zone 8, with regrowth from the base the following spring if roots are mulched.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; named for San Francisco nurseryman Victor Reiter Jr., a longtime favorite in mild-winter West Coast gardens that also performs well in the Gulf South.

directions: Victor Reiter produces abundant, outward-facing, soft tangerine-orange flowers along gracefully arching branches, set against plain deep-green, maple-shaped foliage on a vigorous, medium-to-large shrub. The arching growth habit shows off the flowers to good effect from below, making it a strong choice for a raised bed, large container, or the back of a tender mixed border. Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune back hard in early spring to control size and encourage the densest flowering growth. It blooms over a long season from spring through fall and is a reliable hummingbird draw, but is killed back hard by frost and should be treated as a cut-back perennial or overwintered container plant outside the mildest zones.

common_name: Patrick Synge Abutilon (Trailing Orange-and-Red Flowering Maple)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; a sister seedling to 'Kentish Belle' from the same Abutilon megapotamicum cross, sharing its lax, scrambling habit best suited to training against a wall or support.

directions: Patrick Synge bears pendent, bell-shaped flowers with dark red calyces surrounding bright orange petals, held on slender, lax stems that scramble and arch rather than stand fully upright, much like its sister cultivar 'Kentish Belle'. It reaches its best display trained against a warm wall, trellis, or other support, where the trailing wands of bloom can be shown off vertically, though it also works well spilling from a raised bed or large hanging container. Grow in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helpful during peak summer heat. It flowers from spring through fall, drawing hummingbirds throughout, and is reliably killed back by frost in zone 8, resprouting from the base the following season if roots are mulched.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in bright, partial shade; Savitzii is a dwarf, heavily variegated selection best treated as a foliage plant, holder of an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Savitzii is grown almost entirely for its striking foliage — small, maple-shaped leaves so heavily marbled in cream and white over green that some leaves appear nearly all-white — on a naturally dwarf, dense, slow-growing plant that stays far more compact than most abutilon cultivars. Sparse, small, peach-to-salmon bell flowers appear occasionally but are secondary to the foliage display, and the palest leaves can scorch in strong, direct sun, so bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun gives the best color without burning. Grow in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil, and pinch stem tips regularly to keep the naturally compact habit dense and well-shaped in a container or as a small accent shrub. Like other tender abutilons, it is killed to the ground by hard frost and is best overwintered indoors or in a sheltered spot outside zones 9 and 10.
sources: Logee's Plants for Home and Garden
